evidence.claims: Most quantitative claims check against results.txt (b8 gains +0.014/+0.042, b40 within 0.002, Halton b8 rank 0.98, farthest b4 0.99, full-front 75/76/47, Halton stall to 75). Two wording overclaims: 'worse than all 300 random orders at every budget to 30' (README.md:41) is false at B=16, where one random seed scores below lexicographic (checked: sum(r<=lex)=1, ties 0); 'intervals just above random's' (README.md:42) is false for random-start farthest-point, whose interval [0.814,0.829] overlaps random's [0.799,0.816]. Limitations are honest and prominent ('single draws', 'one small table'). No prior-work citation for space-filling designs or for random-vs-grid search, so the reader is not told this is a known effect.
evidence.fitness: A researcher can rerun and extend it in minutes (stdlib, one table). But the finding (lexicographic grid order is poor at small budgets; quasi-random/maximin orders help) is the standard design-of-experiments result (Halton 1960; Johnson, Moore and Ylvisaker 1990 maximin designs; Bergstra and Bengio 2012, JMLR 13:281, random search beats grid), here confirmed on one 80-point toy table with deterministic orders as single draws. Useful as a harness default fix, not a new research result.
evidence.domain: A senior DSE researcher accepts the metric (hypervolume ratio, fixed reference, exact HV) and the honest single-table caveat, but would flag: no citation of the DoE literature the question belongs to; deterministic orders compared to a random distribution without any randomisation of axis labelling or scrambled Halton/Owen scrambling, which would give them an interval on this same table; 'latin' is a greedy nearest-to-target batch, not a Latin hypercube; comparisons of stochastic orders use separate unpaired bootstrap intervals rather than a difference interval. Departs from DoE practice in those ways.

verdict: Correct and reproducible, but below the bar on claims and verification. results.txt regenerates byte-identical, and an independent stdlib implementation (own normalisation, Pareto filter, exact 3-D hypervolume, Halton and lexicographic orders, disjoint random seeds) matches the 12-design front, the lexicographic and Halton curves to three decimals and the random means within the author's intervals. Two README sentences say more than the data: lexicographic is not worse than all 300 random orders at B=16 (one is lower), and the random-start farthest-point interval overlaps random's at B=8. Tests check the curve against a slow definition but leave Halton, Latin and the bootstrap untested (3 of 4 mutants survive). As research, the effect is the textbook design-of-experiments result, uncited, on one 80-point toy table with deterministic orders as single draws; it is a sound harness-default fix, not a new result. Median 2; misses the bar on claims (2) and verification (2).
